common_name: Jewel of Desert Amethyst Ice Plant

planting.note: Set out rooted plugs in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this compact series is bred to stay tighter and denser than older seed-grown Delosperma cooperi.

directions: Set out rooted plugs in spring into lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; winter wet, not cold, is what kills this species. Jewel of Desert Amethyst forms an unusually tight, dense evergreen mat of small succulent leaves, noticeably more compact than Fire Spinner or Mesa Verde, and is smothered from June into September in two-inch pink flowers with a glowing bright-purple center. Bred as part of a named series selected for a smaller, denser growth habit and improved cold hardiness compared to older Delosperma cooperi seed strains, it holds up well to zone 5 winters when drainage is sharp. Use it in rock gardens, gravel plantings, and green roofs where a slow, restrained spreader is preferred over more vigorous ice plant selections.

common_name: Jewel of Desert Garnet Ice Plant

planting.note: Set out rooted plugs in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; good winter drainage matters more to survival than cold air temperature.

directions: Plant rooted plugs in spring in lean, sandy or gritty soil with excellent drainage, in full sun. Jewel of Desert Garnet carries two-inch, daisy-shaped flowers that shade from deep garnet-red at the petal tips down through pink toward white-and-yellow centers, a richer bicolor effect than the plain rose-pink of the species. The plant forms a dense, ground-hugging mat only a few inches tall and blooms continuously from spring until frost, considerably longer than many hardy succulents. Patented as part of a compact breeding line selected for tighter habit and cold hardiness to roughly zone 5, it is well suited to rock gardens, retaining-wall tops, and hot, dry parking-strip plantings where taller groundcovers would flop or rot.

common_name: Jewel of Desert Peridot Ice Plant

planting.note: Set out rooted plugs in spring in average to sandy, low-fertility, well-drained soil in full sun; rich soil or shade weakens flowering and invites rot.

directions: Plant rooted plugs in spring into average, well-drained, low-fertility or sandy soil in full sun. Peridot is the yellow-flowered member of the Jewel of Desert line, producing starry, two-inch, bright lemon-yellow blooms with white centers over a dense, compact mat of green succulent foliage from late spring through early fall. It is the only yellow selection among the Jewel of Desert colors already represented in this dataset, which lean pink and red, giving it distinct value for color-planning a xeriscape bed. Reliably hardy to about zone 5 where winter drainage is sharp, it is prone to rot and disease in humid or poorly drained sites and should never be planted where water stands.

common_name: Wheels of Wonder Golden Wonder Ice Plant

planting.note: Set out rooted plugs in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; this series was bred for larger flowers and a more vigorous spread than the compact Jewel of Desert line.

directions: Plant rooted plugs in spring into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun. Golden Wonder is part of the Wheels of Wonder breeding line, bred by the same program behind the Jewel of Desert series but selected for noticeably larger blooms and a more vigorous, faster-spreading habit rather than a tight, compact mat. Its wide, glistening flowers open a warm golden yellow shading toward orange at the base, covering the low succulent foliage from late spring through early fall. Because it spreads considerably wider than Jewel of Desert selections or Mesa Verde, it works well as a fast-filling groundcover on slopes and hot, reflected-heat strips where quick coverage matters more than restraint.

common_name: Wheels of Wonder White Wonder Ice Plant

planting.note: Set out rooted plugs in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; provide sharp drainage through winter, since wet soil during dormancy is more damaging than cold air.

directions: Plant rooted plugs in spring into lean, gritty soil with excellent drainage in full sun. White Wonder is the pure-white-flowered member of the vigorous Wheels of Wonder series, opening large, glistening, daisy-like blooms with no colored eye or blush from early summer to fall over a dense, evergreen mat of small succulent leaves. It fills in noticeably faster and wider than the compact Jewel of Desert cultivars, making it a useful clean-white option for mass plantings, retaining walls, and hot, dry strips where a fast-spreading groundcover with season-long bloom is wanted. Like other Delosperma, flowers close on overcast days and reopen fully in bright sun.

common_name: Margarita Rosita Portulaca (AAS-Winning Rose-Pink Moss Rose)

planting.note: Surface-sow seed after the last frost into warm, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; do not cover the fine seed, which needs light to germinate.

directions: Surface-sow seed into warm soil after the last frost in a lean, well-drained, full-sun site; the fine seed needs light and warmth to germinate reliably. Margarita Rosita was named an All-America Selections bedding-plant winner for its early, uniform flowering and large, fully double, glowing rose-pink blooms that open well ahead of older portulaca seed strains. Plants form a tight, compact mound of fleshy, needle-like foliage rather than sprawling loosely, making the color show dense and self-contained. Like all moss rose, it thrives on neglect in hot, dry, lean soil and needs only occasional water once established, continuing to bloom through the hottest stretches of summer.

common_name: Margarita Peppermint Portulaca (Bicolor Striped Moss Rose)

planting.note: Surface-sow seed after the last frost into warm, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; do not cover the fine seed, which needs light to germinate.

directions: Surface-sow seed into warm soil after the last frost in a lean, well-drained, full-sun site, since the fine seed germinates only when exposed to light. Margarita Peppermint stands out from the plain-colored moss roses already in this dataset with its candy-striped bicolor blooms: bright pink petals brushed and streaked with darker fuchsia in an irregular peppermint pattern, no two flowers marked quite alike. Plants form the same compact, early-flowering mound typical of the Margarita series, covering themselves in large double blooms through the heat of summer. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once established and prefers to be kept on the dry side in lean or sandy soil.

common_name: Happy Hour Deep Red Portulaca (Mounded Non-Trailing Moss Rose)

planting.note: Sow or transplant after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Happy Hour was bred to flower under shorter day length than older strains, so it blooms earlier and more uniformly in spring.

directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun. Unlike the sprawling, trailing moss rose types already in this dataset, Happy Hour Deep Red grows into a tidy, upright mound with narrow green leaves, holding its shape in containers and beds rather than spreading loosely outward. It was bred to set flower buds under shorter day length than traditional portulaca, so it blooms earlier in the season and more evenly across the whole planting rather than opening sporadically. Large, fully double, deep red blooms cover the plant through summer heat, closing at night and on heavily overcast days like other moss rose. Its dense, well-branched habit resists breakage in shipping and holds up well in mass plantings and borders.

common_name: Happy Hour Banana Portulaca (Mounded Non-Trailing Moss Rose)

planting.note: Sow or transplant after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this compact, mounded selection holds its shape rather than trailing.

directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun. Happy Hour Banana carries soft, creamy banana-yellow double flowers over a compact, well-branched, upright mound rather than the cascading habit of trailing moss rose series, making it easier to keep tidy in beds and mixed containers. Part of a breeding line selected to flower reliably under the shorter day lengths of early spring, it comes into bloom sooner and more evenly than older seed-grown portulaca. Fleshy, drought-storing foliage lets it shrug off Gulf Coast summer heat and dry spells with only occasional watering, flowering continuously into fall.

common_name: Samba Pink Bicolor Portulaca (Trailing Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant transplants after the last frost into well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Samba was bred to set flower buds 10-14 days earlier than typical trailing portulaca.

directions: Plant transplants after the last frost into well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun. Samba Pink Bicolor is a vegetatively propagated, trailing portulaca series distinguished by two-toned blooms: bright magenta-pink petal edges radiating inward to glowing golden-yellow centers, a sharper bicolor contrast than the solid-colored trailing cultivars already in this dataset. It sets its first buds ten to fourteen days earlier than most trailing moss rose, giving color sooner in hanging baskets and window boxes. Cascading stems can carry dozens of blooms at once on a single hanging basket, and like other portulaca the flowers open fully only in direct sun, closing on cloudy days and toward evening. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and needs only occasional watering through summer heat.

planting.note: Plant transplants after the last frost into well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Samba was bred to set flower buds 10-14 days earlier than typical trailing portulaca.

directions: Plant transplants after the last frost into well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun. Samba Purple is a vegetatively propagated, trailing portulaca prized for a rich purple-magenta flower color rarely seen in seed-grown moss rose, held over the same cascading, fleshy-leaved stems typical of the series. It buds up ten to fourteen days earlier than standard trailing portulaca, filling hanging baskets with color sooner in the season. A single ten-inch hanging basket can produce dozens of blooms at a time through the hottest, driest stretch of summer, opening fully only in bright sun and closing on overcast days and at night. Once established it needs very little supplemental water, thriving in the same lean, sharply drained conditions that suit other Gulf Coast succulent annuals.
